Values come from ProductionCost's machine step table and the block entities' public constants.
manual.geometallurgy.appendix.power.l2: The three furnaces are priced per recipe: the reduction furnace has whole reagent-driven routes at 0 FE/t, the electrolysis furnace molten-salt mode caps at 600 FE/t, and the displacement furnace is always 0 FE/t. The per-recipe list is on “Metallurgy: three routes” under Chemistry, advanced!
Below is the whole MolRecipes table (including the rule-generated reactions): index, equation, kind, machines, rate, power draw. The coefficients are integer ratios solved by the balancer, not equivalents typed by the author.

manual.geometallurgy.appendix.substances: Below is every substance in the Chemical table: name, id, formula, phase, molar mass and whether it is a solute. The id is also a search key — typing sodium_chloride and typing “sodium chloride” are the same thing.
A “species” search result opens that substance's recipe details directly (the same screen the tech tree uses).
manual.geometallurgy.appendix.techtree.l: The tech tree is another full-screen view: nodes are substances, edges are reactions; double-click a node or press E to see that substance's recipe details. The “Tech tree” button in the top bar opens it at any time, and so does the line below.
A “species” search result opens that same detail screen — three entrances lead to one place.

manual.geometallurgy.chem.acidbase.l1: Chemistry is built on three chains: native sulfur → sulfur dioxide → sulfur trioxide → sulfuric acid; halite → chlor-alkali → hydrochloric acid / caustic soda; nitrate minerals and sal ammoniac → nitric acid / ammonia → ammonium salts. Acid + base → salt + water, carbonate + acid → salt + CO₂ + water, metal oxide + acid → salt + water: these families are balanced by rules, the coefficients are not hand-written.
manual.geometallurgy.chem.acidbase.l2: Solution electrolysis is priced per reaction: each electrolysis reaction carries its own FE per mol of reactant (water 150, chlor-alkali 260, potash 300, manganate 180, hydrogen fluoride 520) instead of one flat constant. The machine charges for the mol it actually advances, and when power runs short it shrinks the advance to fit the budget — no “react first, fail to pay later”.
manual.geometallurgy.chem.acidbase.l3: The table below lists the five electrolysis reactions and their prices, computed from the reaction table.
manual.geometallurgy.chem.acidbase.title: The acid–base–salt chains
manual.geometallurgy.chem.chemistry.l1: Mining, beneficiation and smelting end at casting. What remains is chemistry: turning concentrates into salts, acids and bases, and pulling the rare earths out of them.
manual.geometallurgy.chem.chemistry.l2: Chemistry needs only two machines - the reaction vessel and the mixer. Both take mol metering buckets (15 mol each) and both run integer-balanced reactions; they differ only in stirring and ratio control.
manual.geometallurgy.chem.chemistry.l3: A machine holds a single mixed-mol account, not a set of fluid tanks. An input face pulls buckets from the container against it, drains them and pushes the empties back; an output face fills empty buckets with the selected phase and pushes them out.
manual.geometallurgy.chem.chemistry.l4: Every face must be marked input or output with the engineering configurator; all six start disabled. The six cells on either side of the screen are those face switches.
manual.geometallurgy.chem.chemistry.l5: Reactions are matched one by one: the account composition is read, every equation with all reactants present is picked, and each advances by its limiting reagent. The mixer can first blend the A and B input faces by ratio and then match reactions - use it to suppress side products.
manual.geometallurgy.chem.kinetics.l1: Every reaction states its rate (batches/tick), where one batch is one whole equation; the machine's throughput cap scales it: reaction vessel / mixer 1 batch/t, electrolysis furnace solution mode 0.5 batch/t.
manual.geometallurgy.chem.kinetics.l2: A catalyst is both a gate and a speed-up: without it the reaction does not run at all, and with it the rate is multiplied by 4. Stirring works the same way: reactions that need stirring only run in the mixer (they barely happen in the vessel), and stirring multiplies the rate by 1.25.
manual.geometallurgy.chem.kinetics.l3: Reversible reactions have a 5% dead band: |Q − K| ≤ 5%·K counts as at equilibrium and nothing moves, so the reaction cannot oscillate around the balance point every tick. Progress is quantised down to a thousandth and leftovers stay in the ledger. The table below lists these constants straight from code.
manual.geometallurgy.chem.kinetics.title: Rate and equilibrium
manual.geometallurgy.chem.roasting.l1: High-temperature roasting / decomposition (thermal dehydration, oxalate roasting, limestone calcination) needs the volatiles to leave continuously, which a sealed reaction vessel cannot provide. These are classified as “roasting”, and the only machine in that set is the reduction furnace.
manual.geometallurgy.chem.roasting.l2: This also closed a real defect: caustic soda dehydrating and “sodium oxide + water → caustic soda” used to be two opposite one-way reactions with very different rates; sharing one tank they cancelled each other forever and left a fixed pinch of sodium oxide behind. With roasting classified separately the room-temperature vessel no longer runs it. The table below lists which machines each reaction kind allows.
manual.geometallurgy.chem.roasting.title: Roasting belongs to the reduction furnace
manual.geometallurgy.chem.routes.l1: The route is decided by the mineral chemistry, not by a fixed chain.
manual.geometallurgy.chem.routes.l2: Reduction Furnace (carbothermic) - the generalist. 4 iron blocks + 4 bricks + 1 furnace + 1 coal block. Oxide powder goes in and carbon takes the oxygen. Cheap reagent, medium power, medium yield and grade.
manual.geometallurgy.chem.routes.l3: Electrolysis Furnace (molten salt) - expensive and clean. 4 copper blocks + 2 redstone blocks + 2 iron blocks + 1 lightning rod. About ten times the power of reduction for the highest yield. Reactive metals (aluminium, magnesium, calcium) only go this way. An anode and a cathode pair are required, each wearing separately.
manual.geometallurgy.chem.routes.l4: Displacement Furnace (wet) - almost no power. 4 copper blocks + 2 glass + 2 iron blocks + 1 furnace. But every unit of metal eats a unit of a more reactive metal: iron for copper, zinc for silver. Yields a tank of brine.
manual.geometallurgy.chem.routes.l5: Picking a route: hematite is carbothermic only; malachite takes reduction or displacement; fluorite only goes through molten electrolysis.
manual.geometallurgy.chem.routes.l6: High-purity ingots can be cast back into vanilla ingots to rejoin vanilla crafting.
manual.geometallurgy.chem.routes.title: Three Routes
manual.geometallurgy.chem.title: Chemistry, advanced!
manual.geometallurgy.granted: Field Manual granted — right-click to open.
manual.geometallurgy.industry.battery.l1: Recipe: 5 copper ingots + 3 iron ingots + 1 redstone.
manual.geometallurgy.industry.battery.l2: It has no direction: every tick it draws from sources in range and feeds consumers at the same time, each way at 50% loss.
manual.geometallurgy.industry.battery.l3: Each listed device has its own rate, cycled with - and +; rate 0 means no supply. Up to 16 devices, transfer capped at 64 FE/t, and the list scrolls with the wheel.
manual.geometallurgy.industry.bucket.l1: The reagent bucket holds chemicals: 15 mol each. Its colour follows the contents, blended over the mol share of each species, and near-colourless mixtures come out grey-white.
manual.geometallurgy.industry.bucket.l2: Buckets never go into a machine screen. Put them in a chest against a machine face: mark that face input and they are pulled out, mark it output and it receives the filled product buckets.
manual.geometallurgy.industry.bucket.l3: A filled bucket lists total mol, the equivalent number of buckets and total mass, then every component; a mixture is listed by mol share.
manual.geometallurgy.industry.bucket.l4: The creative tabs list a full bucket of every reagent so reactions can be wired up directly. In survival these buckets can only be produced by the reaction vessel or the mixer.
manual.geometallurgy.industry.bucket.l5: Buckets come in four materials: iron holds only water and salts, glass resists acids and oxidizers, lead resists acids and fluorides (hydrofluoric acid needs lead or ceramic), and ceramic resists everything at the highest cost. The vessel and mixer refuse to drain a bucket its material cannot hold, and refuse to fill an empty bucket the product would corrode; the screen reports it.
manual.geometallurgy.industry.bucket.l6: Besides buckets there are barrel blocks (iron/glass/lead/ceramic, 60 mol = 4 buckets each): right-click with a bucket to pour in or draw a bucket out, right-click empty-handed for a reading. Machines move mol to and from barrels directly across a face without going through buckets, and breaking a barrel drops its contents as buckets instead of losing them.
manual.geometallurgy.industry.casting.l1: High-purity ingots can be cast back into vanilla ingots to rejoin vanilla crafting.
manual.geometallurgy.industry.casting.l2: The bar is 90% base metal - the ones named fine. Below that you cannot cast, because too much impurity means the result could not honestly be called that metal.
manual.geometallurgy.industry.casting.l3: 70% base metal is the threshold to be named after it; below that it is simply an alloy ingot.
manual.geometallurgy.industry.casting.l4: Alloy ingots are material only for now, with no special use yet.
manual.geometallurgy.industry.centrifuge: Recipe: 4 iron blocks + 2 copper blocks + 2 glass + 1 redstone block.
Splits feed into heavy and light phases by density.
The cut density is adjustable in the GUI (1.5 to 8.0, default 3.0) at 8 mB/t; spin (power) sets sharpness - slower means blurrier - and the cut decides which density splits off.
manual.geometallurgy.industry.crusher.l1: It grinds slurry or solids down. On slurry input it outputs powder; when that powder later reaches the magnetic separator its ideal field window narrows sharply, and low-grade powder yields far lower metal purity when smelted.
manual.geometallurgy.industry.crusher.l2: Job one - grinds slurry into powder at 8 mB/t, costing 16 x (1 + Mohs/4) FE per mB (up to 256 FE/t drawn per tick; magnetite 40, diamond 56 FE/mB). Composition is carried over unchanged and purity does not rise.
manual.geometallurgy.industry.crusher.l3: Job two - two item slots on its face grind whole items: charcoal to 4 carbon powder. The input slot only takes grindables; the output only gives.
manual.geometallurgy.industry.crusher.l4: The two slots also obey the six-face roles: faces marked in feed the input, faces marked out give the output, the same setting the slurry uses.
manual.geometallurgy.industry.crusher.l5: Both jobs share the same power. Powder narrows the separator's ideal field window - that is the price of grinding finer.
manual.geometallurgy.industry.displaceme: Role: wet displacement. Draws no power at all (0 FE/t); 60 ticks per batch, and the cost is a metal more reactive than the target.
The price is that every unit of metal eats a unit of a more reactive metal (iron for copper, zinc for silver) and yields a tank of brine.
Best when you happen to have cheap reactive metal on hand.
manual.geometallurgy.industry.drill.l1: Two extractors: the Vein Extractor yields solid ore items, the Fluid Vein Crusher yields mixed slurry.
manual.geometallurgy.industry.drill.l2: Both need a drill bit, and bits are consumables.
manual.geometallurgy.industry.drill.l3: Four tiers: stone / iron / gold / diamond.
manual.geometallurgy.industry.drill.l4: Hardness decides what it can bite: the bit hardness must be at least the mineral Mohs value, otherwise nothing comes out (the status shows bit too soft). Toughness decides whether it shatters, and durability is wear - so diamond is the hardest and the shortest-lived.
Electrodes are consumables; one rod lasts a number of batches.
Carbon rod - the cheapest electrode, lasting 8 batches.
Tungsten / molybdenum rod - tungsten lasts 64 batches, molybdenum 40; long electrolysis runs depend on them.
manual.geometallurgy.industry.electrolys: Role: molten electrolysis. Each recipe carries its own draw (160 FE/t base, 600 cap); 120 ticks per batch. The solution side charges per reaction (150 - 520 FE per mol of reactant). Still the most power-hungry of the three routes.
It needs an anode and a cathode pair, each wearing down separately: a carbon rod is cheap but lasts 8 batches, tungsten 64, molybdenum 40.
Reactive metals (aluminium, magnesium, calcium) and fluorite only go this way, in exchange for the highest yield of the three.
manual.geometallurgy.industry.faces.l1: A freshly placed machine has all six faces closed - it will not pull anything in, nor push anything out. Which face does what is your call.
manual.geometallurgy.industry.faces.l2: Way one: right-click the machine, then click each face through input / output / byproduct / disabled.
manual.geometallurgy.industry.faces.l3: Way two: the Engineering Configurator (1 iron ingot + 2 redstone + 1 paper). Shift-right-click a machine to copy its six faces, then Shift-right-click another machine of the same type to write them in; Shift-right-click air to clear.
manual.geometallurgy.industry.faces.l4: Copying only works between machines of the same type - crusher to crusher, magnetic separator to magnetic separator. Crossing types is refused outright, because the two face-role enums number their values differently; forcing it would only give you a machine with six wrong faces.
manual.geometallurgy.industry.faces.l5: One reminder: give a smelter its slag port first, or the first batch will run until the slag tank is full and stop there.
manual.geometallurgy.industry.flow.l1: Ore → (vein extractor) → concentrate → (crusher) → concentrate powder → (reaction vessel / centrifuge) → compound → (reduction furnace | electrolysis furnace) → metal ingot → (crusher) → metal powder.
manual.geometallurgy.industry.flow.l2: Left to right is also the order of this book: extractors at the ore end, crusher and magnetic separator / centrifuge in dressing, reaction vessel and mixer in chemistry, the three furnaces in smelting. Pages with a recipe draw a crafting grid at the end.
manual.geometallurgy.industry.flow.l3: The table below shows where each machine sits on that line and what it draws — power is read from the block entities' public constants, never copied by hand.
manual.geometallurgy.industry.flow.title: One line, start to finish
manual.geometallurgy.industry.fluid.l1: The second route is the Fluid Vein Crusher, this mod's own line: it yields no ore items at all, grinding the whole body into a suspension and piping it into an internal tank.
manual.geometallurgy.industry.fluid.l2: That slurry carries every component of the ore - main mineral, gangue and companion traces, nothing left out.
manual.geometallurgy.industry.fluid.l3: From there the whole chain runs on fluid: the crusher grinds it finer, the separator splits by magnetism, the centrifuge splits by density, and only then does a smelter turn it back into metal.
manual.geometallurgy.industry.fluid.l4: The payoff is that the hard parts of real ore - grade, grain size, impurities, companion phases - all have somewhere to live.
manual.geometallurgy.industry.fluid.l5: The two routes do not conflict: mine solid ore for a quick start, then move over to the fluid line.
manual.geometallurgy.industry.fluid_extr: Role: mines virtual veins and grinds them into mixed slurry in an internal tank. Draws 1024 FE/t and yields 100 mB (= 0.1 mol) every 20 ticks, i.e. 20480 FE per harvest / 204800 FE per mol.
It also needs a drill bit, with the same hardness threshold as the solid extractor.
It is the head of the entire fluid chain: every later machine eats the slurry it produces.
Burns coal or charcoal to generate power and push it to neighbouring machines - the entry-level generator, outputting 64 FE/t.
It burns coal, charcoal or lava buckets. Output 64 FE/t, internal buffer 12800 FE, up to 256 FE pushed out per tick.
This mod pushes power rather than letting machines pull it: machines never reach out for power, so a generator must touch its consumer, or touch a machine that is already powered.
One generator roughly runs one machine flat out; add more to run more at once.
manual.geometallurgy.industry.mixer.l1: The mixer is the reaction vessel plus stirring plus precise ratio control: the same catalyst slot and mol account, six roles per face (Off / A in / B in / Liquid out / Gas out / Solid out, cycled by clicking), plus an A:B ratio.
manual.geometallurgy.industry.mixer.l2: Material pulled in through the A and B faces is first blended into the account at that ratio and only then reacts. The ratio is set by a continuous slider on the screen (0..100%), 50% by default.
manual.geometallurgy.industry.mixer.l3: Reactions that need stirring happen only in the mixer; conversely, with the right ratio the limiting reagent is used up exactly, leaving side reactions without feedstock - that is how it keeps unwanted products out.
manual.geometallurgy.industry.mixer.l4: A typical chain: feed rare earth oxide and hydrochloric acid at 1:6 for rare earth chloride, then precipitate light and heavy rare earths separately with oxalic acid.
Role: carbothermic or metallothermic reduction. Each recipe carries its own draw: fuel-fired routes (blast furnace, reverberatory, native-metal melting) use no power at all, while the electric-furnace ones run at 80 FE/t base (192 cap); 100 ticks per batch.

The reagent can always be carbon-based (coal / charcoal / carbon powder / carbon rod); a metal is only an optional alternative. Only the displacement furnace requires a metal, and it must be more reactive than the target.
The generalist of the three, with middling yield and grade; oxide ores such as hematite can only go this way.
manual.geometallurgy.industry.sensor.l1: Recipe: 2 iron ingots + 1 copper ingot + 1 redstone.
manual.geometallurgy.industry.sensor.l2: It is parasitic: break the host and it shatters with it, so no dangling sensor is ever left pointing at a machine that is gone.
manual.geometallurgy.industry.sensor.l3: One sensor per machine is enough.
Recipe: 4 redstone blocks + 4 iron blocks + 1 copper block.
Splits feed into concentrate and tailings by magnetism. Field strength follows draw: 64 FE/t is nominal field 1.0.
It takes slurry and powder alike; powder runs dry separation with a narrower, fiddlier window.
manual.geometallurgy.industry.solid.l1: The first route is the Vein Extractor, which follows the vanilla convention: it outputs vanilla ore items.
manual.geometallurgy.industry.solid.l2: Its job is to let this mod fit the vanilla pace - it works with no other machine from this mod, and can hook into vanilla materials.
manual.geometallurgy.industry.solid.l3: The price is that it only gives vanilla minerals: use this machine alone and you never reach the mod's own content.
manual.geometallurgy.industry.title: Industrialisation, go!
manual.geometallurgy.industry.vein_extra: Role: mines the chunk's virtual vein and yields vanilla ore items, into 9 output slots.
Draws 1024 FE/t and harvests once every 20 ticks (20480 FE per item). Needs a drill bit whose hardness is at least the mineral's Mohs value.
The closer to the vein core, the more each harvest yields.
manual.geometallurgy.industry.vessel.l1: The reaction vessel is the simplest chemical container: one catalyst slot, one mol account and one output phase selector. It draws no power.
manual.geometallurgy.industry.vessel.l2: Every tick it scans the account for runnable equations and runs them, but it does not stir. Some reactions (hydrogen with chlorine, for instance) hardly happen without stirring, and the screen says so.
manual.geometallurgy.industry.vessel.l3: Output faces carry their own phase: click that face to cycle Off -> In A -> In B -> Liquid out -> Gas out -> Solid out. Each output face moves only its own phase into buckets or barrels; the rest stays on the account. There is no global output-phase button.
manual.geometallurgy.industry.vessel.l4: It is cheap and runs continuously, but it cannot control ratios, so side reactions run along with the wanted one.
manual.geometallurgy.machine.battery.fac: No face roles, devices join via the wireless sensor
manual.geometallurgy.machine.battery.in: Generating devices with a wireless sensor
manual.geometallurgy.machine.battery.out: Consuming devices with a wireless sensor
manual.geometallurgy.machine.coal_genera: No face roles: vanilla container rules — fuel from any side, empty buckets only out of the bottom
manual.geometallurgy.machine.displacemen: Ore powder + a metal more reactive than the target
Metal ingot + a tank of salt solution
manual.geometallurgy.machine.fluid_extra: Only output faces (push slurry), no input face
Virtual vein + the drill bit fitted to the machine
Mixed slurry, injected into the internal tank
manual.geometallurgy.machine.smelter.fac: Input / product / slag faces; all three furnaces share one face-role set
manual.geometallurgy.nav.hint: ← / → turn · wheel turns · click a bookmark to change chapter
manual.geometallurgy.preface.abundance.l: Rarity is no longer decided by real-world grade alone. Three knobs are each discretised into five tiers and do not interfere: spawn chance S1..S5 only decides whether the mineral appears at all, centre grade G1..G5 only decides what volume fraction it occupies at the centre, and body size B1..B5 only decides how big the body is.

In the real world the rarest ore is about 10⁶ times rarer than the most common one; here the spread is deliberately compressed to about 55× (0.40×0.30 ÷ 0.06×0.0365) so rare minerals land in a playable range. That is a game correction, not a real grade.

The star rating in this book uses only two axes: spawn chance × mid centre grade, split logarithmically into 1..5 stars. The most common (S1·G1) gets 1 star, the rarest (S5·G5) gets 5, the rest scale in between. The column “★★★☆☆ S3·G2·B3” in the ore table is “stars + the three tier codes”.
The tier values are in the table below (read from OreTier): S is spawn chance, G is the centre grade range, B is the extent multiplier.
manual.geometallurgy.preface.deposit.l1: Which rock an ore body lives in, and which shape it takes, comes from its deposit parameters: magnetite and hematite occur in sedimentary and plutonic rock, wolframite in plutonic and metamorphic rock, diamond only in plutonic pipes. The rock itself also evolves with (seed, coordinates, epoch), so veins move as epochs pass.
manual.geometallurgy.preface.deposit.l2: There are seven shapes: disc, band, pipe, lode, pod, disseminated, placer. Each gives three semi-axis ratios (strike / secondary / thickness), an orientation mode and a grade falloff exponent — a lode is rich only along its centre (falloff 1.8), while a disseminated body stays fairly rich over a wide area (0.8).
manual.geometallurgy.preface.deposit.l3: “How far from the centre” uses exactly one formula: project the offset onto the three semi-axes to get the normalised distance q; q ≥ 1 is outside the body, and inside the q < 0.30 core the grade is not discounted. The table below is read straight from OreBodyShape.
manual.geometallurgy.preface.intro.l1: This mod generates no real ore blocks underground.
manual.geometallurgy.preface.intro.l2: Instead there are virtual veins: a body of ore computed deterministically from the world seed and chunk coordinates. It exists only as a calculation and occupies no block.
manual.geometallurgy.preface.intro.l3: Three benefits: the underground stays intact instead of being riddled with ore textures; the same vein can be mined again and again instead of hunting for new ones; and shape, grade and companion phases can follow real deposit parameters.
manual.geometallurgy.preface.intro.l4: Find veins with the Mineral Prospector and mine them with an extractor. Extractors come in two routes, described below.
manual.geometallurgy.preface.intro.title: What a Virtual Vein Is
manual.geometallurgy.preface.ores.l1: Below are all 34 virtual ores, computed from OreMineral and OreTier: name (language file), shape, star rating with the three tier codes, main output (the mineral's valuable substance) and companions (naturally carried substances, from a few permille to a few percent).
manual.geometallurgy.preface.ores.l2: Main output and companions are substance names, not mineral names — one ore yields one main substance plus a few companions, which is exactly what makes magnetic separation and centrifugation able to separate something.
manual.geometallurgy.preface.ores.title: The 34 minerals
manual.geometallurgy.preface.prospect.l1: Veins are not blocks - they are virtual ore bodies in the ground. Each body has a core and a rim: grade is highest at the core, and falls off outward, sometimes to a few percent of the core value.
manual.geometallurgy.preface.prospect.l2: Short right-click opens a picker; scroll to choose the mineral you want to prospect for.
manual.geometallurgy.preface.prospect.l3: Long right-click scans on release and reports the nearest ore-body core of that mineral, with its bearing, distance and depth.
manual.geometallurgy.preface.rule.l1: A vein is not a block that gets written into a chunk — it is a pure function of (world seed, coordinates, epoch). Same seed, same position, same epoch: reload the save as often as you like and the ore body comes out identical. That is why no real ore blocks are generated underground, and why chunk files store no vein data at all.
manual.geometallurgy.preface.rule.l2: Because nothing is persisted, the prospector recomputes on every scan: it does not read a cache, it evaluates the function at that point right now. So the prospector is always live — mine a block and the next scan reports the remaining amount.
manual.geometallurgy.preface.rule.l3: Machines are the opposite: on its first harvest a vein extractor stores the computed ore body together with the epoch number, and then keeps mining from that survey until the epoch changes — that is what “a machine keeps its survey until the next epoch” means.
manual.geometallurgy.preface.rule.l4: The epoch length is fixed by three EpochClock constants (table below): 24000 ticks/day × 10 days = 240000 ticks, roughly 3.3 real hours, and it only advances while a player is online. Each chunk also carries a deterministic offset of 0..one period, so different chunks switch veins at different moments — no tidy “re-roll line” across the map.
manual.geometallurgy.preface.rule.title: Generation rule: a pure function

manual.geometallurgy.usage.rxn_formula_n: Reaction usage is computed the same way: S = 20·A + 8·B + ΣR. A = 1 if every reactant is reachable from the ore roots; B = 1 if every product is; ΣR = the sum of the involvement counts of the (deduplicated) products. A and B are walked on ReactionGraph with every machine available, R is counted from MolRecipes; the list below is sorted by S.
manual.geometallurgy.usage.sub_formula_n: Usage is computed from the data: S = 2·R + 3·D + 10·A. R = reactions it takes part in (as reactant or product, counted once each); D = downstream reactions (reactions that consume it); A = 1 if it can be derived from the ore roots with every machine available, else 0. R is counted from MolRecipes and A is walked on ReactionGraph; the list below is sorted by S, click an entry to open its page.
